passages.title: The Arithmetic of the Corner Shop
passages.passage:
A. Ask most people why small shops close and they will reach for the obvious villain: the supermarket down the road, the online giant, the landlord who doubled the rent. All of these matter. Yet economists who study small enterprises point to a quieter culprit, one that rarely makes the news because it is not dramatic. It is the slow mismatch between what a business earns and when it earns it. A bakery may be perfectly profitable on paper and still fail, because its bills arrive on the first of the month while its customers pay in dribs and drabs over thirty days.

B. This gap between profit and cash is the first thing that surprises new owners. Suppose a café sells a coffee for three pounds that costs one pound to make. The margin looks handsome. What the figure hides is everything that must be paid before the first cup is poured: the lease, the machine, the staff who stand ready through the empty hours between breakfast and lunch. Fixed costs, as they are called, do not shrink when custom is slow, and it is these, far more than the price of milk, that decide whether the shutters stay up. Only when the daily takings clear that fixed threshold does a single sale begin to add anything to the owner's pocket.

C. No sooner has an owner grasped this than a second lesson arrives: scale cuts both ways. A chain can negotiate cheaper flour, spread the cost of an accountant across fifty branches, and survive a bad month in one town because a good month elsewhere covers it. A single shop has none of these cushions. On the other hand, the chain must standardise, and standardisation is precisely what a small business need not do. It can know its regulars by name, change the menu on a Tuesday because a supplier turned up with unexpected plums, and turn a passing enthusiasm into a product by Friday. Had the corner shop tried to compete on price, it would have lost years ago; that it competes on nimbleness is the reason it is still there.

D. Then there is the question of what an owner's time is actually worth. Many sole traders never put their own wage into the accounts, so the business appears to make money when, in reality, it is being subsidised by seventy-hour weeks at a rate no employee would accept. Economists call this the opportunity cost — the salary the owner is quietly forgoing elsewhere — and its omission is the single most common reason a shop that "does well" leaves its owner poorer each year.

E. None of this is an argument against opening a shop. It is an argument for opening one with the sums done honestly. The most durable small businesses tend to share three habits: they keep a reserve equal to at least two months of fixed costs, they price for the quiet weeks rather than the busy ones, and they treat the owner's time as an expense from day one. What they offer that no spreadsheet can capture is the reason customers walk past a cheaper alternative to reach them — and that, in the end, is the only margin that cannot be undercut.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes a cost that owners commonly leave out of their accounts?
questions.explanation: Section D says many sole traders never put their own wage into the accounts, and names this missing item the opportunity cost.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) gives an example of a small business changing what it sells at very short notice?
questions.explanation: Section C describes a shop that can change the menu on a Tuesday because a supplier arrived with unexpected plums, and turn an idea into a product by Friday.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) lists the practices shared by small businesses that last?
questions.explanation: Section E says the most durable small businesses share three habits and then lists them: a two-month reserve, pricing for quiet weeks, and counting the owner's time as an expense.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why supermarkets and online retailers are driving small shops out of business
The less obvious financial reasons why small businesses survive or fail
How large chains use their size to negotiate lower prices from suppliers
Practical advice on attracting regular customers to a café
questions.explanation: The passage opens by setting aside the "obvious villains" and then examines the quieter causes: cash timing, fixed costs, scale and the owner's unpaid time. The chains and the customers are details within that argument.

questions.q: What does the writer mean by "the only margin that cannot be undercut" in the final sentence?
options: The gap between a product's selling price and the cost of its ingredients
The two-month reserve that protects a shop through its quiet weeks
Customers' attachment to a shop, which a cheaper rival cannot price away
The extra hours an owner works without paying themselves a wage
questions.explanation: The sentence follows "the reason customers walk past a cheaper alternative to reach them". A rival can beat a shop's prices but cannot undercut loyalty, so that loyalty is the margin the writer has in mind, not a figure in the accounts.

questions.q: The word "nimbleness" in section C is closest in meaning to
options: the ability to adapt quickly
the lowest prices in the area
long opening hours
friendly personal service
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts competing on price with competing on nimbleness, right after examples of a shop changing its menu and its products within days. Nimble means quick and light on one's feet; here, quick to adapt.

questions.q: According to the writer, a rise in the price of milk matters less to a café's survival than its fixed costs do.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section B says fixed costs, far more than the price of milk, decide whether the shutters stay up. The statement matches this.

questions.q: Most small businesses in the writer's country close within their first three years.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage discusses why shops close but never gives a figure for how many close or how quickly. With no information either way, the answer is Not Given.

passages.title: Small Boxes, Long Journeys
passages.passage:
For most of the space age, a mission was an event. Years of design went into a single spacecraft, which was launched once, on a rocket that was thrown away, towards a target it would never be able to revisit. [1] The cost of failure was so enormous that engineers built in redundancy upon redundancy, which made every craft heavier, which made the rocket bigger, which made the whole enterprise dearer still.

That logic has begun to unwind. [2] A university department that could never have afforded a place on a rocket thirty years ago can today book a corner of a shared launch for less than the price of a laboratory instrument. What was once the preserve of a handful of national agencies is now open to start-ups, schools and, in a few cases, individuals.

The consequences for science are subtle rather than spectacular. A single large observatory can see farther than a swarm of small ones, and nobody expects a shoebox to photograph the rings of Saturn. [3] Twenty cheap satellites watching the same storm from twenty angles, or a dozen probes dropped into a comet's tail, produce a kind of knowledge that a lone, precious instrument cannot: knowledge of how things vary. Not until the price of a launch fell did it become possible to ask such questions at all.

There are costs, of course, and not only financial ones. Low orbit is filling up. [4] Astronomers complain that streaks of reflected sunlight now cross their long exposures, and the risk of collision rises with every launch. Whether the benefits of cheap access outweigh the clutter it creates is a question the field has only just started to take seriously.

What seems certain is that the age of the single, irreplaceable mission is passing. [5] It is the engineers who are learning to accept the occasional loss, and the scientists who are learning to think in populations rather than in individuals, who are shaping the next chapter. Had the old model persisted, the sky would be quieter — and a great deal less would be known about it.

Choose from the sentences A–G the one which fits each gap. There are two extra sentences you do not need to use.

A. Yet there are questions that a single instrument, however powerful, is simply the wrong tool to answer.
B. Its successor will not be one grander programme but a scattering of smaller, riskier and more frequent ones.
C. The first human landing on another planet is now expected within the lifetime of today's students.
D. Nothing could be repaired, replaced or retried once the countdown reached zero.
E. Thousands of small satellites, many of them no longer working, now share a band of space that was almost empty two decades ago.
F. Rockets whose first stages fly back and land have cut the price of reaching orbit dramatically, and satellites have shrunk to the size of a loaf of bread.
G. Most of these instruments are assembled by the same three manufacturers.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: The gap sits between a craft launched "once" on a rocket "thrown away" and the sentence about the enormous cost of failure. D explains why failure was so costly: nothing could be repaired, replaced or retried.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: "That logic has begun to unwind" needs a sentence saying what changed. F gives the two changes — reusable rockets and tiny satellites — that make the cheap shared launch in the next sentence possible.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: The sentence before concedes that a single large observatory sees farther; A's Yet turns the argument round, and the sentence after gives the questions (how things vary) that only many small instruments can answer.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: "Low orbit is filling up" is expanded by E's thousands of satellites in a once-empty band of space, which in turn explains the astronomers' streaks and the collision risk that follow.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: Its successor in B refers back to "the age of the single, irreplaceable mission"; the smaller, riskier missions it describes lead into engineers accepting the occasional loss.

questions.q: Why does the writer say that "nobody expects a shoebox to photograph the rings of Saturn"?
options: To admit the limits of small satellites before arguing that their value lies elsewhere
To argue that small satellites have made large observatories unnecessary
To show that photographing Saturn is no longer a useful goal for science
To explain why university departments prefer to share a launch
questions.explanation: The remark is a concession: the writer grants what small satellites cannot do, then uses "Yet" and the storm example to show the different kind of knowledge they can produce. It weakens neither large observatories nor the Saturn goal.

questions.q: The phrase "the preserve of" in the second paragraph is closest in meaning to
options: something restricted to a particular group
something protected from damage
something invented by
something feared by
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts what was once limited to "a handful of national agencies" with what is "now open to" start-ups and schools. A preserve here is an activity kept for one group alone.

questions.q: The writer believes the problem of orbital clutter has already been examined thoroughly by researchers.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says the question is one the field has only just started to take seriously, which contradicts the idea that it has been thoroughly examined.

passages.title: What Travelled With the Silk
passages.passage:
A. The popular picture of an ancient trade route is a single caravan setting out from one end of a continent and, months later, arriving at the other. Almost no one made such a journey. Goods travelled far; people, on the whole, did not. A bale of cloth might pass through a dozen pairs of hands, each merchant carrying it only as far as the next market he knew, selling it on at a small profit and turning for home. The route was a relay, not a marathon, and its length was the sum of many short, familiar trips rather than one heroic expedition.

B. What decided where those trips went was rarely the shortest line on a map. It was water. Caravans followed strings of oases across deserts, and the distance between one well and the next set the size of the load an animal could carry. Where rivers ran in the right direction, cargo left the road altogether. On the coasts, the seasonal winds mattered more than any harbour: a ship that missed the turning of the monsoon might wait half a year for the next one. The geography of trade, in other words, was written by rainfall and wind long before any ruler drew a border across it.

C. Cities grew wherever a route was forced to pause. A mountain pass that closed in winter, a river that had to be crossed by ferry, a stretch of desert that could only be entered with a fresh supply of water — each created a place where goods piled up, where merchants waited, and where someone could make a living by feeding, lodging and taxing them. Some of these halts became great cities whose wealth depended entirely on the traffic passing through; when the traffic shifted, the city withered, sometimes within a single generation.

D. The cargo that mattered most was frequently the cargo nobody had paid for. Along with the silk and the spices went the techniques for making paper, the method of casting a particular kind of metal, a new way of tuning a stringed instrument, and stories that surface, subtly altered, in the folk tales of peoples thousands of kilometres apart. Religions moved along the same paths, carried by merchants who prayed at each stop and by monks who found in the caravan the safest way to travel. So, less happily, did disease; a route that could carry a rumour from one end of a continent to the other could carry a plague just as efficiently.

E. Why did the great overland routes fade? Not, as is often said, because ships were suddenly found to be faster; sailors had been carrying goods along the coasts for as long as caravans had crossed the interior. What changed was the balance of cost and risk. A single ship could carry the load of hundreds of animals and pass through the hands of one merchant rather than a dozen, and every pair of hands the cargo avoided was a toll, a bribe or a theft it also avoided. Once the sea became reliably cheaper, the halts along the old roads lost their reason to exist, and the relay quietly stopped being run.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains why some cities lost their wealth quickly?
questions.explanation: Section C says some halts became cities whose wealth depended entirely on passing traffic, and when the traffic shifted, the city withered, sometimes within a generation.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) argues that a common explanation for the decline of the overland routes is mistaken?
questions.explanation: Section E rejects the idea that ships were "suddenly found to be faster" — as is often said — and offers cost and risk as the real reason.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes how natural conditions determined the direction a route took?
questions.explanation: Section B says water, oases, rivers and seasonal winds decided where trips went: the geography of trade was written by rainfall and wind.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) mentions something harmful that spread along the routes?
questions.explanation: Section D ends with disease: a route that could carry a rumour could carry a plague just as efficiently.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
options: Ancient trade routes were chains of short journeys, shaped by geography and carrying far more than goods
Faster ships were the main reason that overland trade came to an end
Merchants in ancient times regularly travelled the full length of a continent
Great cities on the trade routes were founded by rulers in order to collect taxes
questions.explanation: Each section develops one part of this picture: the relay (A), water and wind (B), cities at the halts (C), unpaid-for cargo (D) and why the relay stopped (E). The other options contradict sections A, C and E.

questions.q: What does section D imply about how merchants spread religion?
options: They were paid by religious leaders to carry beliefs to new lands
They spread their faith simply by practising it wherever they stopped
They were forbidden to travel with monks in the same caravan
They regarded religious objects as the most valuable goods they carried
questions.explanation: Religions were "carried by merchants who prayed at each stop": the merchants were not missionaries but travellers whose everyday worship, seen at halt after halt, spread the faith. Nothing in the text supports payment, a ban or a sale of religious goods.

questions.q: The word "withered" in section C is closest in meaning to
options: expanded rapidly
shrank and lost its strength
changed its name
moved to a new site
questions.explanation: A city that had depended on passing traffic lost that traffic; like a plant without water, it withered, that is, shrank and weakened.

questions.q: The writer believes that rulers' borders determined the course of most ancient trade routes.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section B says the geography of trade was written by rainfall and wind long before any ruler drew a border across it, which contradicts the statement.
